To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

RmXer is a light-driven proton pump with the opposite direction of ion transport to BR, and that the inward proton transport activity of RmXer was associated with the formation and decaying of the M intermediate.

we functionally and spectrally characterized a novel member of the xenorhodopsing clade, which is a light-driven inward proton pump, and proposed a putative mechanism for its light-driven inward proton pumping activity.

we functionally and structurally characterized a new member from a marine bacterion Rubricoccus marina, which belongs to the xenorhodopsing clade, and found that it is a light-driven inward proton pump.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new member of microbial rhodopins, which shows light-driven inward proton pumping activity.
the characterization of a new XeR, RmXe, which shows light-driven inward proton pumping activity.

the characterization of a new microbial rhodopsin from a marine bacteriium and provides a new member of microbial rhodopins with light-driven proton pumping activity, which will be a useful model system for further studies of microbial rhodospins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
RmXer is a light-driven inward proton pump, but its photocycle is different from that of BR.
RmXer is the second member of the microbial rhodopsin family to exhibit light-driven inward proton pumping activity.

the light-driven inward transport activity of RmXer is a result of the unique properties of RmXr, including the opposite direction of retinal composition change, the opposite direction of acid-induced spectral shift, the different pKa values of the retinal Schiff base and its counterion, and the different intermediates involved in the photocycle.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
RmXer, as a new member of XeR clades, is a light-driven inward proton pump and the direction of ion transport is opposite that of BR.
RmXeor PoXeRs are the first examples of the microbial rhodopsin that show the inward proton transport activity.
RmXeor PoXeR are light-driven inward proton pumps, which share common features with the outward proton pump, BR, but also show some differences.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the XeR family is a new class of light-driven proton pumps with an opposite proton transport direction to that of other well-studied microbial rhodopsin classes.

the light-driven inward H+ transport activity of RmXer is not a unique characteristic of PoXeRs but is a common feature of the entire XeR clades, which may play a significant role in the adaptation and/or survival of marine bacteria in the light.
the light-driven "in" and "out" proton transport activities of XeR and BR are not determined by their retinal configuration, but rather by the direction of the proton transport.
